notes.meaning: Issachar had four sons: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. These four brothers became the fathers of the main clans in the tribe. Their names match earlier records in Numbers, showing that Israel preserved its family history carefully.

Tola was Issachar's firstborn, and his sons became heads of major family houses. In the days of King David, their descendants numbered 22,600 brave warriors. Even though Tola's name meant a small worm, God raised up mighty soldiers from his family.

Izrahiah and his sons were all chiefs who led another branch of Issachar. Together, their clans supplied 36,000 troops for battle. Their numbers grew unusually large because they had many wives and children, fulfilling God's promise to make Abraham's offspring plentiful.

All the fighting men across the clans of Issachar added up to 87,000 brave soldiers. This official total showed how strong and prepared the tribe was during Israel's kingdom years. It proved God's faithfulness in turning one man's sons into a large, protective army.

The record turns to Benjamin and names three sons: Bela, Becher, and Jediael. Earlier scriptures list ten sons, but this chapter focuses on the three main branches whose lines survived down to David's time. Benjamin had suffered terrible losses in earlier civil wars, yet God preserved these leading houses.

Bela's family branch produced five leaders who headed their own clans. In their official family records, they counted 22,034 mighty men ready for war. These soldiers carried on the courage for which Benjamin was well known.

Becher had nine sons who grew into influential family leaders. Some of their names, such as Anathoth and Alemeth, later became the names of famous towns in Benjamin's territory. Their family roll included 20,200 skilled fighters ready to defend the nation.

Jediael's line is traced through Bilhan to seven chiefs, one of whom shared the name of Ehud, Israel's famous judge. This branch numbered 17,200 soldiers fit for battle. Together, these numbers showed how God rebuilt Benjamin after the tribe was once nearly destroyed.

Shuppim and Huppim came from Ir, while Hushim was descended from Aher. These short notes preserve smaller Benjamite clans that were not listed with the three main brothers above. Some ancient readers saw Hushim as a hidden mention of the tribe of Dan, whose own list is otherwise missing.

Naphtali's four sons are listed as Jahziel, Guni, Jezer, and Shallum, all grandsons of Jacob's wife Bilhah. This is a very short family note, giving only the first generation. Naphtali's territory later became Galilee, where the Lord Jesus did much of His teaching and healing.

The genealogy of Manasseh begins with Asriel and Machir, born through an Aramean concubine, a secondary wife. Machir fathered Gilead and married into Benjamin's tribe. The text also mentions Zelophehad, who became famous because he had only daughters, leading to a special law allowing daughters to inherit family land.

Machir's wife Maacah gave birth to Peresh and Sheresh, whose sons included Ulam and Rekem. Ulam's son Bedan was counted among the prominent leaders of Gilead. These verses show how Manasseh built strong households that took root in the land.

Gilead's sister Hammolecheth gave birth to Ishhod, Abiezer, and Mahlah. The family of Abiezer was well known because Gideon, one of Israel's greatest deliverers, came from it. Shemida's sons are also listed, showing other important households within Manasseh.

Ephraim's line is traced through Shuthelah down several generations to Ezer and Elead. These men were killed by local men of Gath during a livestock raid while the family lived near Philistine borderlands. This tragic battle happened long before the Exodus while the original patriarch Ephraim was still alive.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars believe this raid happened after Israel had already settled in Canaan, and that the name Ephraim here refers to the tribe as a whole rather than the original patriarch.

notes.meaning: Ephraim wept for many days over his fallen sons, and his relatives came to comfort him in his deep grief. Later, his wife gave birth to another son whom he named Beriah, meaning 'in trouble,' because of the sorrow that had struck his home. God kindly gave new life to the family, even though the painful memory remained.

Beriah's descendant Sheerah was an energetic woman of faith who built or fortified Lower and Upper Beth-horon, along with Uzzen-sheerah. These towns guarded important mountain roads in central Canaan. Her great building work earned her an enduring name in Israel's history.

The family line continues down through Rephah and several generations to Elishama, who served as prince of Ephraim during the wilderness years. His grandson was Joshua son of Nun, Moses' trusted helper who led Israel into the Promised Land. God guided this family line across centuries to raise up the very leader who completed the nation's journey home.

Ephraim and West Manasseh received rich towns across central Canaan, including Bethel, Gezer, Shechem, Beth-shean, and Megiddo. These towns formed the heartland of the northern tribes. The broad territory showed how generously God kept His ancient promises to Joseph's family.

Asher had four sons—Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah—and a sister named Serah. Beriah's sons were Heber and Malchiel, who founded key branches of the tribe. Asher was blessed with fertile soil and abundant olive oil along the northern coast.

Heber's family branched out through Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham, and their sister Shua. Shomer's sons were Ahi, Rohgah, Hubbah, and Aram. These family heads led their households faithfully and guarded their tribal heritage.

Helem, the brother of Shomer, had four sons, and his eldest son Zophah became the father of eleven sons. This large household added great strength to the northern border of Israel. Their names were preserved as trusted leaders in Israel's records.

Jether and Ulla headed the next groups of Asher's descendants. Their sons were counted among the noble chiefs of the tribe. Even when little is known of their personal stories, God kept their names in the sacred record.

All these men of Asher were respected heads of families, choice warriors, and top commanders. Their military register recorded 26,000 valiant men fit for battle in the days of King David. God honored their quiet loyalty by keeping their names written in Israel's book of remembrance.
